:::{#thm-first-order-condition}
#### First-order necessary condition

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$.
If $\vx^*$ is a [local minimizer](algebra.qmd#def-local-minimizer) of $f$
and the gradient of $f$ exists at $\vx^*$,
then $\vx^*$ is a stationary point of $f$ (@def-stationary-point).

:::

::: proof

Take $\delta > 0$ as in the definition of a local minimizer.
Fix $i \in \cb{1, \ldots, p}$,
let $\vecf{e}_i$ be the vector with $1$ in entry $i$ and $0$ elsewhere,
and let $g_i(t) \eqdef f(\vx^* + t\,\vecf{e}_i)$ for $t \in \reals$.
For $\abs{t} < \delta$, $\norm{(\vx^* + t\,\vecf{e}_i) - \vx^*} = \abs{t}\,\norm{\vecf{e}_i} = \abs{t} < \delta$,
so $g_i(0) = f(\vx^*) \le f(\vx^* + t\,\vecf{e}_i) = g_i(t)$:
$0$ is a local minimizer of $g_i$.
Moving $\vx$ from $\vx^*$ along $\vecf{e}_i$ changes only $x_i$,
so $g_i'(0)$ is the partial derivative $\deriv{x_i} f(\vx^*)$,
which exists because the gradient does.
By @thm-fermat, $\deriv{x_i} f(\vx^*) = g_i'(0) = 0$.
This holds for every $i$, so every entry of the gradient at $\vx^*$ is $0$ (@def-vector-derivative).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-first-order-condition}
#### Using the condition to locate, and to rule out, minimizers

- For $f(\vx) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - 2 x_1$ of @exm-stationary-point,
  any local minimizer must be the stationary point $\tp{(1, 0)}$.
  It is one: completing the square, $f(\vx) = (x_1 - 1)^2 + x_2^2 - 1 \ge -1 = f(1, 0)$.
- For $f(\vx) = e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1$ of @exm-hessian,
  the second entry of the gradient is $e^{2x_1 + x_2} > 0$,
  so $f$ has no stationary point, and so no local minimizer.
- The converse fails: $f(\vx) = x_1^2 - x_2^2$ has gradient $\tp{(2 x_1,\ -2 x_2)}$,
  so $\vzero$ is a stationary point,
  but $f(0, t) = -t^2 < 0 = f(\vzero)$ for every $t \ne 0$,
  so $\vzero$ is not a local minimizer.

:::
